query: Research on refractory multicomponent alloys has emphasized exceptional strength at room and elevated temperatures, while mechanical assessment has relied mainly on compression and has included relatively few tensile studies. WFeNiMo fragments released more chemical energy than tungsten-alloy fragments in thin-steel-target penetration tests, and HfZrTiTa0.53 was reported at 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain. This evidence establishes strength and energetic promise but leaves limited tensile ductility, load-bearing reliability, and processability unresolved. Subject to preserving strength and impact-triggered energy release, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53 that could improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, directional or quantitative outcomes relative to the reported baseline, the applicable temperature, loading mode, and strain-rate limits, prior evidence from the cited studies, and matched compression, tension, and impact tests with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) to the HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy will, by generating a thin gradient nanostructured layer on its surface, enhance tensile ductility and uniform elongation without sacrificing the alloy’s high yield strength and its capacity for impact‐triggered energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 produced by conventional casting/HIP processing that exhibits high yield strength (≈786 MPa) and limited measured tensile elongation (≈13.5% terminal strain) with a microstructure likely containing continuous brittle phase channels.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) aimed at inducing a gradient nanostructure (with nanograins and potential nanotwins) in the surface region (~30–50 μm thickness) while leaving the core unaltered.
generation.conditions: Quasi‐static uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature (strain rate ~10−3 s−1), supplemented by matched compression tests and high‐strain-rate impact tests to verify preservation of strength and impact energy release characteristics.
generation.structural_mediator: A gradient microstructure with ultrafine grains and increased defect densities (e.g. high dislocation and nanotwin densities) forming in situ during SMAT that mediates a progressive yielding response.
generation.mechanism: The gradient nanostructured surface layer promotes heterogeneous plastic deformation by enhancing localized strain hardening. This delays necking and distributes deformation more uniformly, thereby increasing uniform tensile elongation while the bulk’s intrinsic composition retains high strength and impact-triggered energy absorption capabilities.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-processed baseline, the SMAT-treated HfZrTiTa0.53 is predicted to show an increase in uniform tensile elongation by at least ~50–100% (e.g. from ~13.5% to 20–27% uniform elongation) while retaining a yield strength near 786 MPa and exhibiting comparable impact-triggered energy release.
generation.baseline: The original HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy shows high compressive strength and impact energy release but limited tensile ductility with a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa and a terminal strain around 13.5%.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected when the SMAT processing parameters (impact energy, treatment duration, and depth control) are optimized so that the gradient layer is confined to the surface (~30–50 μm) and does not compromise the bulk’s microstructure. The hypothesis is applicable under room temperature and quasi-static tensile loading; strain-rate dependence and behavior at elevated temperatures remain to be established.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies (e.g. PMC5995863::web::021::discussion) have shown that microstructural engineering can improve ductility in similar refractory or high-strength alloys, the application of SMAT to HfZrTiTa0.53 is novel. There is uncertainty regarding the stability of the induced gradient layer during tensile loading and its interaction with the impact-triggered energy release mechanism. Additionally, differences between compression and tension responses (PMC5578249::web::011::3_discussion, PMC10453588::web::000::abstract) raise questions about transferability of surface modifications.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfZrTiTa0.53 samples: one set undergoing the optimized SMAT to generate a ≈30–50 μm gradient nanostructured surface layer, and a control set with standard processing. Perform uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature (strain rate ~10−3 s−1), along with compression and impact tests to compare yield strength, uniform elongation, and energy release characteristics.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and uniform elongation from stress–strain curves.
Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) of the gradient layer and bulk before and after deformation.
Impact energy release measured via instrumented drop-weight or penetration tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if SMAT-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (≥50% increase) in uniform tensile elongation relative to the control, or if the post-treatment samples show a marked decrease in yield strength or impact-triggered energy release compared to untreated samples.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). ABSTRACTSolid solutions are ubiquitous in metals and alloys. Local chemical ordering (LCO) is a fundamental sub-nano/nanoscale process that occurs in many solid solutions and can be used as a microstructure to optimize strength and ductility. However, the formation of LCO has not been fully elucidated, let alone how to provide efficient routes for designing LCO to achieve synergistic effects on both superb strength and ductility. Herein, we propose the formation and control of LCO in negative enthalpy alloys. With engineering negative enthalpy in solid solutions, genetic LCO components are formed in negative enthalpy refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). In contrast to conventional ‘trial-and-error’ approaches, the control of LCO by using engineering negative enthalpy in RHEAs is instructive and results in superior strength (1160 MPa) and uniform ductility (24.5%) under tension at ambient temperature, which are among the best reported so far. LCO can promote dislocation cross-slip, enhancing the interaction between dislocations and their accumulation at large tensile strains; sustainable strain hardening can thereby be attained to ensure high ductility of the alloy. In summary, careful microstructural examination of Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr was carried out in the present study using advanced TEM and APT techniques. The results reveal that the homogenized and slow cooled (~10 °C/min) microstructure (Condition (1)) has an ordered B2 phase as the continuous matrix, interspersed with discrete cuboidal-like pockets of a disordered BCC phase. While this microstructure morphologically resembles the γ (fcc) + γ’ (ordered L12) type microstructure observed in many Ni-base superalloys, it is “inverted” in the sense that the continuous matrix phase is the ordered B2 phase, resulting in limited compressive ductility. The ductility of this alloy was substantially increased via microstructural engineering involving controlled annealing treatments, resulting in a phase inversion. Consequently, the hard, ordered B2 compound that forms the continuous phase in Condition (1) is replaced by the more ductile, disordered, BCC phase in Condition (3). The resultant microstructurally-engineered RHEA not only exhibits high yield strength at room temperature (~1345 MPa) and 600 °C (~1423 MPa), but also substantial compressive ductility at room temperature (>20%).
